articles.title: Following the Footnotes: How Enablement Became a Question of Law
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
The Federal Circuit regularly says that enablement is a question of law based upon underlying facts -- stated again in Satius v. Samsung (Fed. Cir. Oct. 1, 2026), one of about 130 majority opinions restating the rule. The label lets the appellate court decide enablement de novo and largely disregard the jury's verdict. A famous recent example comes from Amgen v. Sanofi, where the jury found the antibody claims enabled, but the district court and then the Federal Circuit set the verdict aside. But, the nineteenth-century Supreme Court generally treated sufficiency of a patent's description as a question of fact for the jury, not a question of law. Wood v. Underhill (1846).
In about 115 of those 130 opinions, the citation chain leads back to one footnote: Raytheon v. Roper, 724 F.2d 951, 960 n.6 (Fed. Cir. 1983). The footnote is one sentence with no reasoning:
Enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112, paragraph 1, is a question of law.
That one sentence is followed by a string-cite of C.C.P.A. opinion-affidavit cases. The string ends with In re Chilowsky (C.C.P.A. 1962), which makes the matter-of-law claim but cites no source of precedent. (I looked at the other cases in the string-cite as well. None of them explains why enablement is a question of law.) The first, and perhaps only, real explanation I found in a Federal Circuit opinion came 37 years after Raytheon, in Judge Lourie's nonprecedential 2021 opinion denying panel rehearing in Amgen. In my view, the court owes an explanation.

articles.title: Rule 17 Real Party in Interest: No Swapping the Original Plaintiff Back After a Tactical Substitution
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal with prejudice of a patent suit against Netflix -- holding that a plaintiff who swapped-in a newly formed LLC to get around a problem with its own corporate status could not swap itself back once the new LLC turned out to lack the right to sue. Rule 17(a)(3) protects the honest mistake about who should be the plaintiff, but the district court found that this one was "done for tactical advantage."
Touchmusic sued Netflix in March 2024, asserting US6182128, which had expired almost six years earlier. But, at the time of filing Touchmusic's corporate rights were suspended under California law, and a suspended company is barred from filing suit. "This did not deter Touchmusic." Rather than dismissing the case, Touchmusic assigned the patent to newly formed Ziklag IP, a Tennessee LLC, and filed an amended complaint to replace Touchmusic with Ziklag as plaintiff. California restored Touchmusic's good standing on April 19, 2024 - one day after the assignment.
The assignment appears complete on its face:
Touchmusic "hereby irrevocably conveys, transfers, and assigns all of Touchmusic's right, title, and interest in and to the Patent to Ziklag IP LLC."
But assignment of patent rights does not typically confer rights to sue for infringement that occurred before the assignment - that right is still held by the prior owner unless expressly transferred.

articles.title: Patent Public Search Login Requirement: No More Anonymous Searching
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
Beginning December 4, 2026, the USPTO’s Patent Public Search tool will require users to sign in with a USPTO account. The notice banner states that users without an account “are encouraged to create a USPTO account in advance.”
Patent Center has been closed to nonregistered guests since September 11, 2025, and the Open Data Portal has required an account since June 18, 2026. The USPTO’s account page also lists Global Dossier among the systems that can’t be used without one. After December 4, no USPTO tool for searching patents or reading file histories will be open to an anonymous visitor.
This change is part of a larger Trump Administration initiative – although it does not appear to be centrally managed. One example that I read in the NYTimes this week is that savings bond holders can no longer reach their TreasuryDirect accounts without first verifying their identity through ID.me. That is the same private service the USPTO uses for Patent Center.
Stanford Professor Lisa Larrimore Ouellette raised the public access issue on LinkedIn, in a post addressed to the USPTO and Director John Squires. She and Jonathan Masur have a patent casebook used at more than 80 law schools, with an exercise that teaches students how to look up patents. After Patent Center and the Open Data Portal were closed to anonymous users, the latest edition pointed students to Global Dossier, which now requires an account too. Now they are scrambling to work out how to teach patent searching while allowing students to work anonymously online.
Patent attorneys have gone through identity verification already to get access to their private client dockets, but the new requirement limits general searching – something the public has done freely online for decades.
It appears that the Patent Public Search requires a simpler (although not simple) registration process of obtaining a USPTO account (as compared to the ID.me process I went through). An account requires name, email, phone number, and mailing address, along with a reCAPTCHA check and agreement to the USPTO’s terms of use. You then have to activate the account by email and set up two-factor sign-in, using an authenticator app or a biometric key. So, if I understand the approach, this is less onerous than the identity verification for accessing other “public” USPTO sources that require either ID.me verification (quite detailed) or mailing in a notarized paper form that the USPTO states may take up to 10 business days.
Each sign-in to the USPTO account requires multi-factor authentication using an authenticator app or a security key, and the agency does not accept an email or text code verification.
For Patent Public Search itself, the agency says the measure “will improve site security, maintains PPUBS efficiency and reliability, and lead to enhanced future features.” The earlier notices say more. For Patent Center, the USPTO wrote that identity verification helps “deter fraudulent filings” and lets the agency monitor data miners. For the Open Data Portal, registration “will improve site security while limiting costly, unregistered bot traffic.” That notice also says that registration will allow the agency to “improve the customer profile and future offerings.”
The European Patent Office has taken a different route (so far). Espacenet and the European Patent Register remain free, and neither asks for an account. The EPO says that both services will deny access to any robots they identify, and the Register limits each user to ten search-related actions per minute. Automated users are sent to Open Patent Services, which requires registration and is free up to 4 GB of data per week.
As someone who operates a website, the amount of scraping and attempted hacking right now is crazy. Presumably, it’s all facilitated using AI that is willing to keep poking and exploring ways around any hurdle. Bots are 99.9% of site requests on my pages, and I won’t be surprised if it goes out another significant digit over the next year. Of course, I’m just one person, not a multi-billion dollar agency with a public mission goal – they should be able to make the data freely and easily available.
To be clear, I’m strongly in favor of having the USPTO data widely available. For the first 20 years of the internet, the USPTO website was one of the most used government sites. And I used it regularly until a few years ago. But it has become largely unusable to anyone who is not tech savvy. In particular, the public search engine created a few years ago is utterly awful for anyone except for skilled searchers. The new non-anonymous security layer adds one more barrier.
The change reminds me of the Patent Office before 1836. Patents were issued without examination, and it fell to a private publisher to tell the public what had been granted. Beginning in the late 1820s, the Journal of the Franklin Institute in Philadelphia ran a notice of every new U.S. patent, with remarks from its editor, Thomas P. Jones, who had briefly run the Patent Office himself. The Patent Office then burned in December 1836. The fire destroyed the records of nearly 10,000 patents, and more than 7,000 were never recovered. For a lost patent like Philos Blake’s 1830 folding toothbrush, the journal’s notice is the only description that survives. See, Scott Guthery, Julie Burke and Michael Risch, Unfettered Invention: How the X Patents Sparked Early American Technology.

articles.title: Summary Judgment Without Claim Construction
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
Edge Systems LLC v. Cartessa Aesthetics, LLC (Fed. Cir. 2026) (non-precedential)
Edge Systems is the company behind the Hydrafacial, and now goes by that name. The treatment is hydradermabrasion - a handpiece that uses suction and a stream of liquid serums to exfoliate and clean the skin. The company has about 36,000 consoles in spas and medical offices, but about 75% of its revenue comes from the serums and tips that those consoles use up.
Edge's US9550052 covers the console side of that arrangement, claiming a "manifold" that connects several bottles of treatment liquid to a single handpiece line and lets the operator select among them. Edge sued Cartessa back in 2020, alleging that Cartessa's competing Skinwave system infringes. The image below is Edge's annotated photo of the Skinwave, with a white box labeled as the claimed manifold.
District Judge Gary Brown (E.D.N.Y.) granted summary judgment of non-infringement without construing the term "manifold" -- concluding that Edge could not prove the white box was a manifold under any construction since its expert had never even opened it up.
On appeal, the Federal Circuit vacated -- holding that the construction has to come first because a reasonable jury could find the manifold element met under Edge's proposed construction ("a closed space with several inlet pipes and one outlet"). The court also affirmed summary judgment that the claims were not shown invalid. It is almost as if some lower courts have become too willing to decide patent cases on their own - without giving credence to the jury system.

articles.title: Texas Patent Filings: Back to the Eastern District
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch

For a few years, the Western District of Texas was the hot spot of patent law. Judge Albright's patent cases were distributed to other judges on the court, and he has now stepped down from the bench. With that change, Texas patent lawsuit filings have moved back to their more traditional home of the Eastern District. The crossover came in August 2023, and the gap has widened since. E.D.Tex. is now taking in about 140 patent cases per month (90-day average), more than five times the 26 per month filed in W.D.Tex. -- which had been at about 95 per month back in mid-2022, most of them filed in Waco.

Inside the Western District, Waco lost almost all of its patent docket -- falling from over 900 cases in 2021 to 34 newly filed cases in 2025 (and 5 through October 2026). Over the same stretch, the Midland/Odessa division went from zero patent cases to over 300, with more than 80% of them assigned to Judge David Counts. Patentees are still looking for a single-judge forum - but not just any single judge, one who knows patent law and gives patent enforcers a fair shot.
